paper_title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. Experiments demonstrate that LoopDVR achieves the best accuracy--parameter trade-offs across dense recognition tasks. Compared with the reference models, it reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, highlighting its effectiveness in compact models.

sections.content: We propose LoopDVR, framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Introduction Dense Visual Recognition (DVR), including object detection [17], instance segmentation [20], and human pose estimation [4], supports broad applications, e.g., autonomous driving [1], robotics [31] and augmented reality [6]. Transformer-based architectures achieve strong performance via attention-based visual representations and iterative query refinement [5, 72]. But deploying these models on edge devices with limited model-size and GPU memory budgets remains challenging. This motivates extensive research regarding parameter efficiency. Existing approaches improve model parameter efficiency through compact architecture designs [8, 41, 49, 70] or knowledge distillation to smaller students [7, 9, 24]. Using shallower or narrower networks is straightforward way to reduce parameter counts. However, it also limits computational depth or representational capacity, and potentially 1 compromises performance, particularly for compact models. This raises question: Can we reduce parameter counts while preserving the original computational structure, enabling parameter-efficient models to achieve performance comparable to full-sized models? Recent studies on looped Vision Transformers, e.g., MiniViT [68] and Raptor [26], offer promising solution. These methods reuse the same Transformer weights across multiple layers within each group. This strategy reduces parameter counts while retaining the original computational structure and maintaining competitive performance. However, these classification-oriented methods perform less effectively on dense recognition tasks. Similar ideas have also been explored in object detection: DEQDet [61] and RecursiveDet [69] reuse decoder layers for iterative query refinement. But both leave the backbone untouched, overlooking the substantial parameter overhead associated with this component. Moreover, directly looping the same weights across layers can disrupt the hierarchical representations and depth-specific behaviors, leading to training instability and performance degradation [68]. To overcome these limitations, we propose LoopDVR, pretrained-model-guided framework for converting dense recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. It applies looped Transformers within both the ViT backbone and the query decoder. To enable effective parameter sharing while preserving depth-specific behaviors, we investigate two key questions: 1) Where to Loop? This concerns identifying layers suitable for parameter sharing while minimizing disruption to the hierarchical representations. We adopt representation-based grouping strategy, which partitions consecutive layers with similar representations into the same sharing group. Furthermore, to better support multi-scale feature construction from the penultimate and final layers, we reserve the terminal block as an independent group. 2) How to Loop? This focuses on enabling the shared network to preserve the depth-specific transformation of different layers. To this end, we use structured initialization, initializing each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its groups terminal layer, which preserves the learned representations of the pretrained model. We further introduce an independent lightweight Loop Adapter for each layer, which performs depth-specific transformation after the shared block. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone before integrating it with the looped decoder for downstream training. We instantiate LoopDVR as LoopDet, LoopSeg, and LoopPose for object detection, instance segmentation, and human pose estimation, respectively. Across four model scales, LoopDVR reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. As shown in Fig. 1, our models achieve the best accuracyparameter trade-offs. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, while LoopSeg-L improves mask AP by 1.0 over its non-looped reference model. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We introduce LoopDVR, pretrained-model-guided conversion framework that combines representation-based grouping, group-end initialization, and feature distillation to enable effective parameter sharing. We design unified looped architecture by reusing Transformer blocks in both the ViT backbone and query decoder with Loop Adapters, achieving exceptional parameter efficiency while preserving computational depth. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LoopDVR on object detection, instance segmentation, and human pose estimation across four model scales, achieving the most favorable accuracyparameter trade-offs. 2. Related Work Transformer-based Dense Recognition. DETR [5] established query-based set prediction for object detection, laying the foundation for Transformer-based paradigm in dense visual recognition [11, 12, 38, 55, 67]. ViDT [57] extended the role of Transformers to feature extraction by pairing vision Transformer backbone with deformable query decoder [72]. This paradigm extends to other dense visual recognition tasks, including instance segmentation with MaskDINO [33] and human pose estimation with EDPose [64] and GroupPose [36]. Subsequent work tailored this architecture to real-time detection. LW-DETR [8] pairs pretrained ViT backbone with shallow decoder, while RF-DETR [49] builds real-time detector based on DINOv2 [43] backbone. DEIMv2 [24] distills DINOv3 [56] features into narrower ViT backbones for real-time detection. EdgeCrafter [37] brings these directions together in compact framework for edge dense recognition. It distills features from detection-specialized teacher into ECViT and reuses the resulting backbone for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation. These advances have made Transformer-based models effective across dense recognition tasks. Yet feature extraction and query refinement still rely on independently parameterized blocks, whose parameter cost remains concern under tight memory budgets. Looped Transformers in Computer Vision. Looped Transformers introduced recurrent paradigm which reduces parameter cost by reusing blocks across depth [14, 32], principle later adopted in computer vision. In Vision Transformers, SReT [54] recursively applies shared Transformer blocks, while MiniViT [68] uses depth-specific transformations to preserve variation across layers that share weights. Raptor [26] introduces the Block-Recurrent Hypothesis and groups consecutive layers by the similarity of their representations in pretrained ViT, approximating each group with recurrent block. Recent studies have extended looped Transformers to image super-resolution [71], multi-view 3D 2 Figure 2. Overview of LoopDVR. Given dense recognition model, (a) Stage 1 groups the layers of the pre-trained ViT backbone based on inter-layer representation similarity and initializes each looped backbone block using the weights of its groups terminal layer. (b) Transformer block parameters are shared within each group, while each layer has Loop Adapter to preserve depth-specific transformations. (c) Stage 2 distills the looped ViT using DINOv3 teacher. (d) Stage 3 post-trains the resulting architecture for dense recognition, combining the looped ViT, the hybrid encoder and the looped decoder. reconstruction [3], visual tracking [44], image and video generation [13, 18], and vision-language models [19, 47]. In object detection, RecursiveDet [69] shares decoder parameters across box refinement stages, while DEQDet [61, 62] formulates query refinement as fixed-point iteration. Together, these studies show that Transformers can build computational depth by repeatedly applying shared blocks. How to exploit this reuse across depth in both the ViT backbone and the query decoder of compact dense recognition model remains underexplored. 3. Method We present LoopDVR, general framework that transforms pre-trained dense visual recognition models into more parameter-efficient looped networks. As illustrated in Fig. 2, LoopDVR reduces parameter cost by reusing Transformer blocks across multiple layers in both the backbone and decoder, while preserving the original computational depth. We first review the common architecture of Transformer-based dense visual recognition models in Sec. 3.1. We then describe the construction of the looped backbone in Sec. 3.2, addressing where to loop through representation-based grouping and how to loop through structured initialization and Loop Adapters. Finally, we describe the adaptation to dense recognition tasks in Sec. 3.3, including backbone distillation, looped decoder construction, and task-specific training. 3.1. Preliminaries: Transformer-based DVR Transformer-based dense visual recognition architecture consists of ViT backbone, hybrid encoder for multi-scale feature fusion, and query-based Transformer decoder with task-specific prediction heads [24, 37]. The ViT backbone extracts visual representations by sequentially processing image patch tokens through Transformer blocks [15]. Starting from the input patch embeddings X(0), the l-th block Bl transforms the preceding token representations X(l1) into X(l) as X(l) = Bl(X(l1)), = 1, . . . , L. (1) Dense visual recognition benefits from multi-scale feature representations [72]. To this end, hybrid encoder transforms the backbone representations into multi-scale features for the decoder [70]. The encoder uses attention to process features within each scale and convolutions to fuse features across scales. Given the final two backbone representations, the encoded features are computed as [37] Fenc = E(X(L1), X(L)), (2) where denotes the hybrid encoder. The resulting features Fenc provide multi-scale visual context for the decoder. Each decoder block contains self-attention among object queries, 3 deformable cross-attention to encoded features guided by reference boxes, and feed-forward network [72]. The updated queries are used to further refine reference boxes and generate task-specific predictions. We instantiate LoopDVR based on representative family of dense visual recognition models, EdgeCrafter (EC) [37], which is built on pretrained ECViT backbones. 3.2. Looped Backbone Construction As shown in Fig. 2 (a), given pretrained ViT backbone, LoopDVR first converts it into looped ViT. The main challenge in this conversion is that naive parameter sharing may disrupt the original hierarchical representations and depthspecific behaviors [68]. To address this challenge, we optimize the looped architecture from two perspectives, i.e., where to loop and how to loop. Specifically, we determine which layers should share parameters based on representational dissimilarity, while using group-end initialization and Loop Adapters to make parameter sharing more effective. Representation-Based Grouping. Directly sharing the weights across different layers disrupts the original hierarchical features. Following Raptor [26], we adopt representationbased grouping, which places adjacent layers with similar representations into the same sharing group. All layers within group reuse Transformer block, while different groups maintain independent block parameters.

Unlike approaches that randomly initialize shared blocks, LoopDVR aims to transform pretrained models to fully leverage their prior knowledge. This raises key question: which pretrained weights should each shared block inherit? For each group, we compare three strategies: copying the weights of its first layer, copying those of its last layer, or averaging the weights across all layers within the group [52, 63]. To examine their effects, we visualize attention maps at the final backbone layer under different initialization strategies, before backbone distillation. As shown in Fig. 4, groupend initialization produces the most discriminative attention patterns among the three strategies, with attention predominantly focused on target objects. This attention pattern also most closely resembles that of the original network. We therefore initialize each shared backbone block with the weights of its groups terminal layer in the same reference backbone. Appendix C.2 provides layer-wise comparisons of attention maps, while the ablation in Sec. 4.2 confirms its advantage after training. Shared Transformer blocks, their Loop Adapters and the projector are optimized jointly. Looped Decoder Construction. Similar to the backbone, the Transformer decoder exhibits clear grouping structure in inter-layer representation dissimilarity, as shown in Fig. 3b. Accordingly, we extend the same group-wise sharing and Loop Adapter design to the decoder, partitioning its refinement layers into KD groups. The prediction heads are also shared along with the Transformer blocks. To determine the grouping, we compute the dissimilarities using trained, non-looped reference models. The resulting decoder partition is consistent across different models and tasks (Fig. S1 in the Appendix), allowing us to adopt unified grouping for all decoders. Since ECViT [37] focuses only on optimizing backbones and decoders require task-specific post-training, we train looped decoders from scratch for downstream tasks. Downstream Task-Specific Training. As illustrated in Fig. 2(d), we integrate the distilled looped ViT with hybrid encoder and the looped decoder for downstream dense recognition tasks. We train the resulting models for object detection, instance segmentation, and human pose estimation using DETR-style bipartite matching and task-specific supervision [5]. For instance segmentation and pose estimation, we initialize the backbone from the trained detector and extend the architecture with query-based mask head and pose head, respectively [27, 33]. Note that implementation details are provided in Appendix A.4. 4. We instantiate these models based on the ECDet, ECInsSeg, and ECPose architectures from EdgeCrafter [37], respectively. Before task-specific training, we distill the looped backbone using unlabeled images from ImageNet1K [51] and COCO train2017 [35]. We then train four model scales for each task on COCO train2017 and evaluate them on COCO val2017. Training is conducted using 4 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. Figure 4. Training Configurations We train LoopDVR through backbone distillation followed by downstream task-specific training, on 4 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. The hyperparameters of downstream taskspecific training are summarized in Table S2. Backbone distillation. We distill the looped backbones on unlabeled images comprising ImageNet-1K [51] and COCO train2017 [35]. The teacher and student receive the same augmented images, with random resized cropping, horizontal flipping, color jitter, grayscale conversion, Gaussian blur, and Mixup [66]. We apply trainable linear projector to each final-layer student patch token and use an MSE loss to align it with the concatenated features of the corresponding patch token from the teachers last two layers. The shared backbone blocks, Loop Adapters, and the projector are jointly optimized using layer-wise adaptive rate scaling (LARS) [65], with linear learning rate warm-up followed by cosine decay. Object detection. We train the complete LoopDet models end to end on COCO train2017 and evaluate them on COCO val2017 [35]. The distilled backbone, hybrid encoder, looped decoder, and prediction heads are jointly optimized using AdamW [39] and an exponential moving average (EMA). We retain DETR-style bipartite matching [5] and the Decoupled Distillation Focal (DDF) and Fine-Grained Localization (FGL) losses of D-FINE [45]. The optimizer settings, augmentation schedules, training durations, batch sizes, and loss weights are summarized in Table S2. Instance segmentation. sections.content: Fig. 6 compares LoopDet-X with three representative parameter compression methods under comparable parameter budgets. For each compression baseline, we start from the same pretrained ECViT checkpoint and integrate the compressed backbone with the hybrid encoder and decoder. All configurations follow the same backbone distillation and downstream detection training protocol described in Sec. A.4. Neuron Merging. We adapt Intra-Fusion [58], which reduces the number of neurons by merging their weights rather than directly removing less important neurons. We apply this method to the backbone FFNs, reducing their hidden dimension from 2304 to 896 while retaining all six attention heads per layer. Specifically, we first select the target neurons using L1 importance scores. We then measure the similarity between neurons using the normalized weights of the two FFN projections and compute an optimal transport map based on their pairwise L1 distances. This map determines how the original neurons are merged into the selected neurons, using uniform marginals and an exact Earth Movers Distance solver. The merging is applied consistently to both FFN projections and the first projections bias, while the output bias remains unchanged. Structured Pruning. We adapt Isomorphic Pruning [16] to ECViT using Torch-Pruning. Unlike neuron merging, this approach directly removes less important structures, such as attention heads and FFN hidden neurons. To compare their importance more reliably, pruning candidates are grouped according to their structural types and ranked within each group using normalized L1 importance scores. We then remove the selected attention heads and FFN neurons, updating the corresponding projections together to maintain consistent dimensions. Each retained attention head has 64 dimensions. The resulting backbone contains 60 attention heads and 13,824 FFN hidden neurons across 12 layers, with an average FFN width of 1152. Low-rank Decomposition. We adapt FLAR-SVD [59], which reduces parameters by approximating large weight matrix with the product of two smaller matrices, . The intermediate dimension, known as the rank, determines the degree of compression. We apply this approach to the backbones QKV, attention output, and two FFN projections. Following FLAR-SVD, we collect activation statistics from ImageNet-1K [51] training images to guide the decomposition and search for suitable ranks for each layer. The decomposition uses stabilized whitening to account for the input feature distribution, while the rank search targets backbone parameter retention ratio of 55%. Among the 48 candidate linear layers, 35 are factorized and 13 remain unchanged. Each factorized layer retains its original bias, without introducing additional activations between the two factors. B.3. Implementation of Depth Conditioning We apply each conditioning mechanism to both the backbone and decoder in Tab. 5, with the hybrid encoder unchanged. All variants retain the same backbone grouping and the two shared blocks executed over four layers. Shared model weights and conditioning parameters are jointly optimized. The unconditioned baseline shares the original normalization parameters within each shared block. The compared mechanisms introduce depth conditioning through scaling, attention mixing, low-rank updates, normalization, or prompts. Depth scaling [26] uses multilayer perceptron attached to each shared Transformer block to map the layer index to channel-wise scales. The weighttransformation baseline follows MiniViT [68]: it uses depthspecific attention head mixing before and after softmax, together with independent LayerNorm parameters; decoder head mixing is confined to self-attention. LoRA [23] adds depth-specific low-rank updates to selected linear transformations, excluding the terminal singleton backbone group. LayerNorm tuning [46] assigns independent gain and bias parameters to each layer. VPT-Deep [28] inserts independent prompts at each layer and discards their outputs afterward; decoder prompts participate only in self-attention. C. Additional Experiments C.1. Effect of Looped Blocks Count To investigate how many shared blocks should be retained for favorable accuracyparameter trade-off, we vary the number of shared blocks in the backbone and decoder. We keep their depths fixed at = 12 and = 4, respectively. For each configuration, we independently determine the group boundaries using the representation-based grouping strategy described in Sec. 3.2, while reserving an independent block for the final backbone layer. In the upper panel of Fig. S2, detection AP increases with the number of shared backbone blocks, but the gains are smaller beyond KB = 6. For example, increasing KB from 6 to 8 adds two shared blocks and 0.8M parameters for gain of only 0.2 AP points. We therefore use KB = 6 as trade-off between accuracy and model size. Figure S2. All LoopDet-S variants use fixed depths of = 12 in the backbone and = 4 in the decoder, and follow the same partitioning method and training protocol, using Loop Adapters. In the lower panel of Fig. S2, detection AP varies only slightly across the tested decoder configurations. The decoder with two shared blocks achieves AP comparable to that of the decoder with independent layers while using fewer parameters. C.2. For each initialization strategy, the looping backbone retains twelve layers, whereas its non-looping counterpart executes one block per group in sequence, yielding six layers. All constructed backbones are visualized immediately after initialization, before backbone distillation. In the nonlooping controls, group-end initialization produces clearer object-related attention structures than group-start initialization, showing that its qualitative advantage is also observable without repeated block execution. The looping variants reveal how these attention patterns evolve across layers. With group-start initialization, early layers exhibit localized responses, while later layers produce spatially smooth maps with little discernible object-related structure, indicating attention collapse.
